danish.title: Syvende bog (1810–11) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Kort efter juleferien fortalte Nikolaj sin mor om sin kærlighed til Sonja og sit faste forsæt om at gifte sig med hende. Grevinden, der længe havde lagt mærke til, hvad der foregik mellem dem, og havde ventet denne erklæring, lyttede til ham i tavshed og fortalte så sin søn, at han kunne gifte sig med hvem han ville, men at hverken hun eller hans far ville give deres velsignelse til et sådant ægteskab. Nikolaj mærkede for første gang, at hans mor var utilfreds med ham, og at hun, trods sin kærlighed, ikke ville give efter. Koldt og uden at se på sin søn sendte hun bud efter sin mand, og da han kom, forsøgte hun kort og køligt at fortælle ham sagens rette sammenhæng i sønnens nærværelse, men ude af stand til at beherske sig brast hun i tårer af forbitrelse og forlod stuen. Den gamle greve begyndte ubeslutet at formane Nikolaj og bede ham opgive sit forehavende. Nikolaj svarede, at han ikke kunne bryde sit ord, og hans far sukkede og blev, tydeligt forvirret, meget hurtigt tavs og gik ind til grevinden. I alle sammenstød med sin søn var greven altid bevidst om sin egen skyld over for ham for at have ødslet familieformuen, og derfor kunne han ikke være vred på ham, fordi han nægtede at gifte sig med en arving og valgte den medgiftsløse Sonja. Ved denne lejlighed var han blot endnu mere levende bevidst om, at havde hans økonomiske forhold ikke været i uorden, kunne man ikke have ønsket Nikolaj en bedre hustru end Sonja, og at ingen andre end han selv med sin Mitenka og sine upraktiske vaner bar skylden for familiens økonomiske tilstand.

Faderen og moderen talte ikke mere til deres søn om sagen, men et par dage senere sendte grevinden bud efter Sonja og bebrejdede med en grusomhed, ingen af dem havde ventet, sin niece for at forsøge at fange Nikolaj og for utaknemmelighed. Sonja lyttede tavst med sænkede øjne til grevindens grusomme ord uden at forstå, hvad der forlangtes af hende. Hun var parat til at ofre alt for sine velgørere. Selvopofrelse var hendes mest elskede ideal, men i dette tilfælde kunne hun ikke se, hvad hun burde ofre, eller for hvem. Hun kunne ikke lade være med at elske grevinden og hele Rostov-familien, men hun kunne heller ikke lade være med at elske Nikolaj og vide, at hans lykke afhang af den kærlighed. Hun var tavs og trist og svarede ikke. Nikolaj fandt situationen uudholdelig og gik hen for at tale ud med sin mor. Først bønfaldt han hende om at tilgive ham og Sonja og give sit samtykke til deres ægteskab, dernæst truede han med, at hvis hun plagede Sonja, ville han straks gifte sig med hende i hemmelighed.

Grevinden svarede med en kulde, hendes søn aldrig havde oplevet hos hende, at han var myndig, at fyrst Andrej giftede sig uden sin fars samtykke, og at han kunne gøre det samme, men at hun aldrig ville modtage den intrigantinde som sin svigerdatter.

Nikolaj eksploderede ved ordet intrigantinde, hævede stemmen og sagde til sin mor, at han aldrig havde ventet, at hun ville forsøge at tvinge ham til at sælge sine følelser, men at hvis det forholdt sig sådan, ville han for sidste gang sige... Men han nåede ikke at udtale det afgørende ord, som udtrykket i hans ansigt fik hans mor til at vente på med rædsel, og som måske for altid ville være blevet et grusomt minde for dem begge. Han nåede ikke at sige det, for Natasja, med blegt og beslutsomt ansigt, trådte ind fra den dør, hvor hun havde stået og lyttet.
»Nikolaj, du vrøvler! Ti stille, ti stille, ti stille, siger jeg dig!...« næsten skreg hun for at overdøve hans stemme.

»Mamma-skat, det er slet ikke sådan... min stakkels, søde skat,« sagde hun til sin mor, der, bevidst om at de havde været på randen af et brud, betragtede sin søn med rædsel, men i stridens stædighed og ophidselse hverken kunne eller ville give efter.
»Nikolaj, jeg forklarer dig det. Gå nu! Hør, Mamma-skat,« sagde Natasja.
Hendes ord var usammenhængende, men de opnåede det formål, hun tilstræbte.
Grevinden, der hulkede tungt, skjulte sit ansigt ved sin datters bryst, mens Nikolaj rejste sig, greb sig om hovedet og forlod stuen.

Natasja gik i gang med at skabe forsoning og lykkedes så vidt, at Nikolaj modtog et løfte fra sin mor om, at Sonja ikke ville blive plaget, mens han til gengæld lovede ikke at foretage sig noget uden sine forældres vidende.

Nikolaj, fast besluttet på, efter at have bragt orden i sine regimentssager, at forlade hæren, vende hjem og gifte sig med Sonja, rejste alvorlig, sorgfuld og i uoverensstemmelse med sine forældre, men som det forekom ham lidenskabeligt forelsket, i begyndelsen af januar for at slutte sig til sit regiment.
Efter Nikolajs afrejse blev tilstandene i Rostov-huset mere trykke end nogensinde, og grevinden blev syg af sjælelig anstrengelse.

Sonja var ulykkelig over adskillelsen fra Nikolaj og endnu mere over den fjendtlige tone, grevinden ikke kunne lade være med at anlægge over for hende. Greven var mere bekymret end nogensinde over sine økonomiske forhold, der krævede en eller anden afgørende handling. Deres byhus og godset nær Moskva måtte uundgåeligt sælges, og for det måtte de rejse til Moskva. Men grevindens helbred tvang dem til at udskyde afrejsen fra dag til dag.

Natasja, der havde båret den første tids adskillelse fra sin forlovede let og endog muntert, blev nu mere og mere urolig og utålmodig for hver dag. Tanken om, at hendes bedste dage, som hun ville have brugt på at elske ham, gik til spilde uden gavn for nogen, pinte hende uophørligt. Hans breve irriterede hende for det meste. Det smerter hende at tænke, at mens hun kun levede i tanken om ham, levede han et virkeligt liv, så nye steder og nye mennesker, der interesserede ham. Jo mere interessante hans breve var, jo mere irriteret blev hun. Hendes breve til ham, langtfra at give hende nogen trøst, forekom hende en trættende og kunstig pligt. Hun kunne ikke skrive, for hun kunne ikke forestille sig muligheden for oprigtigt at udtrykke i et brev bare en tusindedel af det, hun udtrykte med stemme, smil og blik. Hun skrev formelle, ensformige og tørre breve til ham, som hun selv ikke tillagde nogen betydning, og hvis kladder grevinden rettede stavefejlene i.

Der var stadig ingen bedring i grevindens helbred, men det var umuligt at udskyde rejsen til Moskva længere. Natasjas udstyr måtte bestilles, og huset sælges. Desuden var fyrst Andrej ventet i Moskva, hvor den gamle fyrst Bolkonskij tilbragte vinteren, og Natasja var sikker på, at han allerede var ankommet.
Så grevinden blev på landet, og greven tog Sonja og Natasja med sig til Moskva i slutningen af januar.

english.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: Soon after the Christmas holidays Nicholas told his mother of his love for Sonya and his firm resolve to marry her. The countess, who had long noticed what was going on and had been expecting this declaration, listened in silence and then told her son he could marry whom he pleased, but that neither she nor his father would give their blessing to such a marriage. Nicholas, for the first time, felt that his mother was displeased with him and that despite her love she would not yield. Coldly, without looking at her son, she sent for her husband, and when he came she tried — briefly and coolly, in their son's presence — to inform him of the facts. But she couldn't restrain herself and burst into tears of frustration, and left the room. The old count began half-heartedly to lecture Nicholas and beg him to give up the idea. Nicholas replied that he could not go back on his word, and his father, sighing and clearly uncomfortable, soon fell silent and went in to the countess. In all his dealings with his son, the count was always conscious of his own guilt toward him for having wasted the family fortune, and so he couldn't bring himself to be angry at Nicholas for refusing to marry an heiress and choosing the dowerless Sonya. On this occasion he was simply more acutely aware than ever that if their finances hadn't been in such disarray, no better wife for Nicholas than Sonya could have been wished for, and that no one but himself — with his Mitenka and his careless ways — was to blame for their situation.

The father and mother did not bring up the matter again with their son, but a few days later the countess sent for Sonya and, with a cruelty neither of them expected, reproached her niece for trying to catch Nicholas and for ingratitude. Sonya listened silently with downcast eyes, not understanding what was being demanded of her. She was ready to sacrifice everything for her benefactors. Self-sacrifice was her most cherished ideal — but in this case she couldn't see what she should sacrifice, or for whom. She couldn't help loving the countess and the whole Rostov family, but neither could she help loving Nicholas and knowing that his happiness depended on that love. She was silent and sad and made no reply. Nicholas sensed the situation was unbearable and went to have it out with his mother. He first begged her to forgive him and Sonya and consent to their marriage, then he threatened that if Sonya was mistreated he would marry her in secret.

The countess, with a coldness her son had never seen in her before, replied that he was of age, that Prince Andrew was marrying without his father's blessing and he could do the same — but that she would never accept that schemer as her daughter.

Stung by the word schemer, Nicholas raised his voice and told his mother he had never expected her to try to force him to sell his feelings — but that if that was how it was, he would say once and for all... But he didn't have time to say the decisive word whose expression on his face his mother was awaiting with terror, and which might have remained a cruel memory between them forever. He didn't have time to say it because Natasha, with a pale, set face, came in through the door where she had been listening.
"Nicholas, you're talking nonsense! Be quiet — be quiet — be quiet, I tell you!..." she almost screamed, drowning out his voice.

"Mama darling, it's not like that at all... my poor, sweet darling," she said to her mother, who — realizing they had been on the brink of a rupture — looked at her son with terror, but in the stubbornness and heat of the conflict could not and would not back down.
"Nicholas, I'll explain things to you. Go away! Listen, Mama darling," said Natasha.
Her words were incoherent, but they achieved their purpose.
The countess, sobbing heavily, buried her face on her daughter's chest, while Nicholas got up, clutched his head, and left the room.

Natasha set about making peace, and succeeded well enough that Nicholas extracted a promise from his mother that Sonya would not be troubled, while he for his part promised not to do anything without his parents' knowledge.

Firmly resolved — after putting his regimental affairs in order — to resign from the army and return home to marry Sonya, Nicholas left at the beginning of January to rejoin his regiment. He was serious, sorrowful, and at odds with his parents, but convinced, as it seemed to him, that he was passionately in love.
After Nicholas left, things in the Rostov household grew more depressing than ever, and the countess fell ill from the emotional strain.

Sonya was unhappy at being separated from Nicholas and still more so at the hostile tone the countess could not help adopting toward her. The count was more worried than ever by the state of their finances, which demanded some drastic action. The town house and the estate near Moscow would inevitably have to be sold, and for this they needed to go to Moscow. But the countess's illness forced them to keep postponing their departure from day to day.

Natasha, who had borne the first period of separation from her fiance lightly and even cheerfully, now grew more restless and impatient with each passing day. The thought that her best days — which she would have spent loving him — were being wasted to no purpose tormented her constantly. His letters mostly irritated her. It hurt her to think that while she lived only in thoughts of him, he was living a real life, seeing new places and new people that interested him. The more interesting his letters were, the more annoyed she felt. Her letters to him, far from giving her any comfort, felt like a tedious and artificial obligation. She couldn't write, because she couldn't imagine expressing in a letter even a thousandth part of what she could convey with her voice, her smile, and her eyes. She wrote him formal, monotonous, dry letters to which she herself attached no importance, and the countess corrected her spelling mistakes in the rough drafts.

There was still no improvement in the countess's health, but postponing the trip to Moscow any longer was impossible. Natasha's trousseau had to be ordered and the house sold. Moreover, Prince Andrew was expected in Moscow, where old Prince Bolkonsky was spending the winter, and Natasha was sure he had already arrived.
So the countess stayed in the country, and the count, taking Sonya and Natasha, went to Moscow at the end of January.
